paragraphs: Going in to Lise, he found her half reclining in the invalid chair, the one she had been wheeled around in when she couldn’t walk. She did not move to meet him. Her sharp, keen eyes were simply fixed on his face. They had a feverish look, and her face was pale and yellow. Alyosha was amazed at how much she had changed in three days. She was actually thinner. She did not hold out her hand to him. He touched the long, thin fingers lying motionless on her dress, then sat down facing her without a word.
“I know you’re in a hurry to get to the prison,” Lise said curtly, “and Mamma kept you there for hours. She’s just been telling you about me and Yulia.”
“How do you know?” asked Alyosha.
“I was listening. Why are you staring at me? I wanted to listen, so I listened. There’s no harm in that. I’m not apologizing.”
“Are you upset about something?”

“On the contrary, I’m very happy. I’ve just been thinking, for the thirtieth time, what a good thing it is that I turned you down and won’t be your wife. You’re not fit to be a husband. If I married you and gave you a note to take to the man I loved after you, you’d take it, you’d be sure to deliver it, and you’d bring back an answer, too. Even if you were forty, you’d still be carrying my love letters for me.”
She suddenly laughed.
“There’s something spiteful about you, and yet something open-hearted, too,” Alyosha said to her with a smile.

“The open-hearted part is that I’m not ashamed of myself with you. What’s more, I don’t want to feel ashamed with you, only with you. Alyosha, why don’t I respect you? I’m very fond of you, but I don’t respect you. If I respected you, I couldn’t talk to you without shame, could I?”
“No.”
“But do you believe I’m not ashamed with you?”
“No, I don’t believe it.”
Lise laughed nervously again. She spoke rapidly.
“I sent your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch some sweets in prison. Alyosha, you know, you’re quite good-looking! I’ll love you terribly for so quickly letting me not love you.”
“Why did you send for me today, Lise?”
“I wanted to tell you about a longing I have. I’d like someone to torture me. Marry me and then torture me, deceive me and go away. I don’t want to be happy.”
“You’re in love with disorder?”

“Yes, I want disorder. I keep wanting to set fire to the house. I keep imagining how I’ll creep up and set fire to the house on the sly. It has to be on the sly. They’ll try to put it out, but it will go on burning. And I’ll know and say nothing. Ah, what silliness! And how bored I am!”
She waved her hand with a look of disgust.
“It’s your life of luxury,” said Alyosha softly.
“Is it better to be poor, then?”
“Yes, it is better.”

“That’s what your monk taught you. It’s not true. Let me be rich and everyone else poor. I’ll eat sweets and drink cream and not give any to anyone else. Ach, don’t speak, don’t say anything,” she shook her hand at him, though Alyosha had not opened his mouth. “You’ve told me all that before. I know it by heart. It bores me. If I’m ever poor, I’ll murder somebody, and even if I’m rich I might murder someone, maybe. Why sit and do nothing? But do you know, I’d like to reap, to cut rye? I’ll marry you and you’ll become a peasant, a real peasant. We’ll keep a colt, shall we? Do you know Kalganov?”
“Yes.”

“He’s always wandering about, dreaming. He says, ‘Why live in real life? It’s better to dream. You can dream the most delightful things, but real life is a bore.’ But he’ll be married soon all the same. He’s already been making love to me. Can you spin tops?”
“Yes.”

“Well, he’s just like a top. He wants to be wound up and set spinning and then lashed, lashed, lashed with a whip. If I marry him, I’ll keep him spinning all his life. You’re not ashamed to be with me?”
“No.”
“You’re terribly cross because I don’t talk about holy things. I don’t want to be holy. What will they do to a person in the next world for the worst sin? You must know all about that.”
“God will condemn you.” Alyosha was watching her steadily.

“That’s exactly what I’d like. I’d go up, and they’d condemn me, and I’d burst out laughing in their faces. I’d dearly love to set fire to the house, Alyosha, to our house. You still don’t believe me?”
“Why not? There are children of twelve who long to set fire to something, and they do set things on fire, too. It’s a sort of disease.”
“That’s not true, that’s not true! There may be such children, but that’s not what I mean.”
“You take evil for good. It’s a passing crisis. Perhaps it’s the result of your illness.”
“You do despise me, though! It’s simply that I don’t want to do good, I want to do evil, and it has nothing to do with illness.”
“Why do evil?”

“So that everything would be destroyed. Ah, how nice it would be if everything were destroyed! You know, Alyosha, I sometimes think of doing a fearful lot of harm, of doing everything bad. I’d do it for a long while on the sly, and then suddenly everyone would find out. Everyone would stand around and point their fingers at me, and I’d look at them all. That would be awfully nice. Why would it be so nice, Alyosha?”
“I don’t know. It’s a craving to destroy something good or, as you say, to set fire to something. It happens sometimes.”
“I don’t only say it, I’ll do it.”
“I believe you.”
“Ah, how I love you for saying you believe me. And you’re not lying one little bit. But perhaps you think I’m saying all this on purpose to annoy you?”
“No, I don’t think that... though perhaps there’s a little wish to do that in it, too.”
“There is a little. I can never tell you lies,” she declared, with a strange fire in her eyes.

What struck Alyosha above everything was her earnestness. There was not a trace of humor or joking in her face now, though in the old days fun and gaiety never deserted her, even at her most “earnest” moments.
“There are moments when people love crime,” said Alyosha thoughtfully.

“Yes, yes! You’ve said just what I think. They love crime. Everyone loves crime, and they love it always, not just at some ‘moments.’ You know, it’s as though people had made an agreement to lie about it and have lied about it ever since. They all declare that they hate evil, but secretly they all love it.”
“And are you still reading nasty books?”
“Yes, I am. Mamma reads them and hides them under her pillow, and I steal them.”
“Aren’t you ashamed to destroy yourself?”

“I want to destroy myself. There’s a boy here who lay down between the railway lines when the train was passing. Lucky fellow! Listen, your brother is being tried now for murdering his father, and everyone loves it that he killed his father.”
“Loves it that he killed his father?”
“Yes, loves it. Everyone loves it! Everybody says it’s so awful, but secretly they simply love it. I for one love it.”
“There’s some truth in what you say about everyone,” said Alyosha softly.

“Oh, what ideas you have!” Lise shrieked in delight. “And you a monk, too! You wouldn’t believe how I respect you, Alyosha, for never telling lies. Oh, I must tell you a funny dream of mine. I sometimes dream of devils. It’s night. I’m in my room with a candle, and suddenly there are devils all over the place, in all the corners, under the table. They open the doors, and there’s a crowd of them behind the doors, and they want to come in and seize me. And they’re just coming, just seizing me. But I suddenly cross myself, and they all draw back, though they don’t go away altogether. They stand at the doors and in the corners, waiting. And suddenly I have a frightful longing to curse God out loud, and so I begin, and then they come crowding back to me, delighted, and seize me again, and I cross myself again and they all draw back. It’s awful fun. It takes your breath away.”
“I’ve had the same dream, too,” said Alyosha suddenly.
“Really?” cried Lise, surprised. “I say, Alyosha, don’t laugh, this is awfully important. Could two different people have the same dream?”
“It seems they can.”

“Alyosha, I tell you, it’s awfully important,” Lise went on, with truly excessive amazement. “It’s not the dream that matters, it’s your having the same dream as me. You never lie to me, so don’t lie now. Is it true? You’re not laughing?”
“It’s true.”
Lise seemed extraordinarily impressed, and for half a minute she was silent.
“Alyosha, come and see me, come and see me more often,” she said suddenly, in a pleading voice.
“I’ll always come to see you, all my life,” answered Alyosha firmly.

“You’re the only person I can talk to, you know,” Lise began again. “I talk to no one but myself and you. Only you in the whole world. And I talk to you more readily than to myself. And I’m not a bit ashamed with you, not a bit. Alyosha, why am I not ashamed with you, not a bit? Alyosha, is it true that at Easter the Jews steal a child and kill it?”
“I don’t know.”

“There’s a book here in which I read about the trial of a Jew who took a child of four years old and cut off the fingers of both hands, and then crucified him on the wall, hammered nails into him and crucified him. Afterwards, when he was tried, he said the child died soon, within four hours. That was ‘soon’! He said the child moaned, kept on moaning, and he stood there admiring it. That’s nice!”
“Nice?”
“Nice. I sometimes imagine it was I who crucified him. He would hang there moaning and I would sit opposite him eating pineapple _compote_. I’m awfully fond of pineapple _compote_. Do you like it?”
Alyosha looked at her in silence. Her pale, sallow face was suddenly contorted, and her eyes burned.

“You know, when I read about that Jew, I shook with sobs all night. I kept imagining how the little thing cried and moaned (a child of four years old understands, you know), and all the while the thought of pineapple _compote_ haunted me. In the morning I wrote a letter to a certain person, begging him _particularly_ to come and see me. He came, and I suddenly told him all about the child and the pineapple _compote_. _All_ about it, _all_, and said that it was nice. He laughed and said it really was nice. Then he got up and went away. He was only here five minutes. Did he despise me? Did he despise me? Tell me, tell me, Alyosha, did he despise me or not?” She sat up on the couch, with flashing eyes.
“Tell me,” Alyosha asked anxiously, “did you send for that person?”
“Yes, I did.”
“Did you send him a letter?”
“Yes.”
“Simply to ask about that, about that child?”
“No, not about that at all. But when he came, I asked him about it right away. He answered, laughed, got up and went away.”
“That person behaved honorably,” Alyosha murmured.
“And did he despise me? Did he laugh at me?”
“No, because perhaps he believes in the pineapple _compote_ himself. He’s very ill now, too, Lise.”
“Yes, he does believe in it,” said Lise, with flashing eyes.
“He doesn’t despise anyone,” Alyosha went on. “Only he doesn’t believe anyone. If he doesn’t believe in people, then of course he does despise them.”
“Then he despises me, me?”
“You, too.”
“Good,” Lise seemed to grind her teeth. “When he went out laughing, I felt that it was nice to be despised. The child with his fingers cut off is nice, and being despised is nice...”
And she laughed in Alyosha’s face, a feverish, malicious laugh.

“Do you know, Alyosha, do you know, I’d like—Alyosha, save me!” She suddenly jumped from the couch, rushed to him and seized him with both hands. “Save me!” she almost groaned. “Is there anyone in the world I could tell what I’ve told you? I’ve told you the truth, the truth. I’ll kill myself, because I loathe everything! I don’t want to live, because I loathe everything! I loathe everything, everything. Alyosha, why don’t you love me in the least?” she finished in a frenzy.
“But I do love you!” answered Alyosha warmly.
“And will you weep over me, will you?”
“Yes.”
“Not because I won’t be your wife, but simply weep for me?”
“Yes.”

“Thank you! It’s only your tears I want. Everyone else may punish me and trample me underfoot, everyone, everyone, not excepting _anyone_. For I don’t love anyone. Do you hear, not anyone! On the contrary, I hate him! Go, Alyosha. It’s time you went to your brother”; she tore herself away from him suddenly.
“How can I leave you like this?” said Alyosha, almost in alarm.
“Go to your brother, the prison will be shut. Go, here’s your hat. Give my love to Mitya, go, go!”

And she almost forcibly pushed Alyosha out of the door. He looked at her in pained surprise, when he suddenly became aware of a letter in his right hand, a tiny letter folded tight and sealed. He glanced at it and instantly read the address: “To Ivan Fyodorovitch Karamazov.” He looked quickly at Lise. Her face had become almost menacing.
“Give it to him, you must give it to him!” she ordered, trembling and beside herself. “Today, right away, or I’ll poison myself! That’s why I sent for you.”

And she quickly slammed the door. The bolt clicked. Alyosha put the note in his pocket and went straight downstairs, without going back to Madame Hohlakov. He had forgotten her, in fact. As soon as Alyosha had gone, Lise unbolted the door, opened it a little, put her finger in the crack and slammed the door with all her might, pinching her finger. Ten seconds later, she released her finger and walked softly, slowly to her chair. She sat up straight in it and looked intently at her blackened finger and at the blood oozing from under the nail. Her lips were quivering, and she kept whispering rapidly to herself:
“I’m a wretch, wretch, wretch, wretch!”
